newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Kinnock to address road transit issue on Alpine tour.
newsitem.headline: Kinnock to address road transit issue on Alpine tour.

text.p: European Transport Commissioner Neil Kinnock sets out on a four-day lobbying tour on Monday, visiting Austria, Italy and France in an effort to ease trans-alpine road transport tension, a Commission official said.

The issue of alpine transit traffic poses tricky problems for the European Commission and the countries involved, linking the EU's road transport negotiations with Switzerland and road transport policies in Austria, France and Italy.
Switzerland has limited lorry weights to a maximum of 28 tonnes, as opposed to the EU's 40 tonnes, meaning that lorries tend to travel instead through France or Austria to get to or from Italy.

"We have a fairly serious problem looming in that if we do not have a deal with Switzerland, the country will be able to do exactly what it likes in 2005, which will hit Austria and spill over into France and Italy," the official said.

Talks with Switzerland, part of a package of bilateral issues under discussion since early 1995, have stuttered along with the aim of securing EU lorries greater access to, and transit through, Switzerland.

Directly linked to these questions is Switzerland's proposal for a phased abolition of its current 28-tonne limit on all lorries, allowing 34-tonne vehicles onto Swiss roads from the start of 2001 and 40 tonners from 2005.

At the same time, Switzerland would introduce scaled charges for all lorries on its roads reflecting their infrastructure damage and "nuisance cost" -- a figure based on the amount of noise and pollution caused by the vehicle and associated health effects.
Berne's existing agreement with the EU expires in 2005, after which time the country could revamp its rules as it wishes in the absence of a new EU deal.
EU countries also worry that the plan could set a precedent for the EU's own policy, a fear fuelled by the Commission's recent enthusiasm for the idea.

A further complicating factor is the toll regime in place for Austria's Brenner Pass route between Innsbruck and Bolzano in Italy. The Commission has declared the regime illegal because it involves price hikes and differentials which it says are discriminatory to non-Austrian, EU transporters and unrelated to infrastructure costs.

The Commission has sent Vienna a reasoned opinion setting out its objections to the regime -- "the stage at which things get legal" according to the official -- which in particular focus on the way night tolls are imposed.
"Tolls must be linked to infrastructure costs. There is nothing Austria has shown us to say that this is so. The result has been traffic going through Italy and France instead," the official added.
On Monday, Kinnock is scheduled to overfly Austria's Inn valley as a guest of the Austrian government to see for himself the scale of the traffic problem faced by the country.

The Commissioner is in a somewhat awkward position in that on the one hand he has championed differential transport prices in his green paper, COM(95)691, while on the other he must force Austria to comply with existing EU transport legislation and resolve the Alpine transit issue.

"What we are at pains to say to the Austrians is that we understand what Austria has done but we cannot allow it. (Their action) does also makes it difficult for us to make our case to the Swiss," the official added.
Kinnock is due in Rome on Tuesday to discuss the issue with Italian Transport Minister Claudio Burlando and in Paris Thursday to meet the French Secretary of State for Transport Anne-Marie Idrac.
